cases.title: Decompensated Liver Cirrhosis — History Long Case
cases.summary: A 52-year-old three-wheeler driver with abdominal swelling, leg oedema and jaundice, with a long alcohol history.

patient.name: Nimal
patient.opening: Doctor, my belly keeps getting bigger and my eyes have turned yellow.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.purpose: Introduce yourself, confirm identity, get consent and open the consultation.

exchanges.ask: Good morning. I'm one of the doctors on the ward. Could I confirm your name and age, please?
exchanges.reply: I'm Nimal Perera, I'm fifty-two.

exchanges.ask: Thank you, Mr Perera. I'd like to ask you some questions about why you came in and then examine you. Is that all right?
exchanges.reply: Yes, doctor, that's fine.

exchanges.ask: What do you do for work, and who is at home with you?
exchanges.reply: I drive a three-wheeler. I live with my wife and two children.
exchanges.note: Occupation and home support matter later for alcohol history and discharge planning.

exchanges.ask: Could you tell me in your own words what brought you to hospital?
exchanges.reply: My belly has been getting bigger for about two months and my legs are swollen. My wife says my eyes have turned yellow.
exchanges.note: Let the patient finish; the three complaints give you the diagnosis to test.

sections.title: Presenting complaint
sections.purpose: Characterise each symptom: onset, progression, associated features, and what has made it better or worse.

exchanges.ask: Tell me about the swelling of your belly. When did you first notice it?
exchanges.reply: About two months ago. My trousers got tight, and it has slowly grown since.

exchanges.ask: Is it painful?
exchanges.reply: Only a dull heaviness. It is not sharp pain, but it makes me breathless when I lie flat.

exchanges.ask: Have you had any fever with it?
exchanges.reply: No fever, doctor.

exchanges.ask: And the leg swelling. When did that start?
exchanges.reply: A few weeks after the belly. First my ankles, now up to my knees, both sides.

exchanges.ask: Have you noticed the yellow colour in your eyes or skin? How long?
exchanges.reply: The yellow came about three weeks ago. My urine is dark, like tea. The stools are normal colour.

exchanges.ask: Have you been itchy?
exchanges.reply: A little, mostly at night.
exchanges.note: Pruritus with jaundice suggests a cholestatic component.

exchanges.ask: Have you vomited blood or passed black stools?
exchanges.reply: No blood in vomit. My stools are not black.
exchanges.note: Key negative: a variceal bleed changes management completely.

exchanges.ask: Any confusion, or changes in your sleep?
exchanges.reply: My wife says I sleep a lot during the day and am awake at night. I forget things sometimes.
exchanges.note: Day-night reversal is an early sign of hepatic encephalopathy.

sections.title: Systemic review
sections.purpose: Screen other systems and look for complications of liver disease and its causes.

exchanges.ask: Have you lost weight or lost your appetite?
exchanges.reply: I have lost my appetite. My arms and legs look thin even though the belly is large.

exchanges.ask: Any shortness of breath on walking, chest pain or palpitations?
exchanges.reply: A bit breathless on stairs. No chest pain.

exchanges.ask: Have you had any easy bruising or bleeding from your gums or nose?
exchanges.reply: I bruise easily on my arms.

exchanges.ask: Any change in your bowel habit, diarrhoea or constipation?
exchanges.reply: No, normal.

exchanges.ask: Passing urine normally? Any reduction in how much?
exchanges.reply: I am passing less than before, I think.

exchanges.ask: Have you noticed any lumps in your belly, or breast swelling?
exchanges.reply: My chest has become a bit tender and enlarged on both sides.

sections.title: Past medical history
sections.purpose: Look for causes and risk factors for chronic liver disease.

exchanges.ask: Have you ever been told you have diabetes, high blood pressure or high cholesterol?
exchanges.reply: I was told my sugar was a little high two years ago. I never took tablets.

exchanges.ask: Have you ever had hepatitis, or been told your liver tests were abnormal?
exchanges.reply: Nobody told me before.

exchanges.ask: Have you ever received a blood transfusion, had tattoos or needle injections outside hospital?
exchanges.reply: No transfusions or tattoos.

exchanges.ask: Have you been vaccinated against hepatitis B?
exchanges.reply: I don't think so.

sections.title: Past surgical history
sections.purpose: Ask about operations and previous admissions.

exchanges.ask: Have you ever had an operation?
exchanges.reply: No operations.

exchanges.ask: Have you been admitted to hospital before this?
exchanges.reply: Once, years ago, with a fever. Nothing to do with my liver.

sections.title: Drugs and allergies
sections.purpose: Prescribed and over-the-counter drugs, herbal remedies and allergies.

exchanges.ask: Are you taking any regular tablets or medicines?
exchanges.reply: No prescribed medicines.

exchanges.ask: Do you take painkillers, herbal medicines or any traditional preparations?
exchanges.reply: I take paracetamol sometimes for back pain. Also a herbal tonic from the shop for energy.
exchanges.note: Ask about quantity of paracetamol and any hepatotoxic remedies.

exchanges.ask: Any allergies to medicines?
exchanges.reply: None.

sections.title: Family and social history
sections.purpose: Take a non-judgemental alcohol history and screen for other risks.

exchanges.ask: Do you drink alcohol? What do you drink and how much?
exchanges.reply: I drink arrack most evenings, about a third of a bottle.
exchanges.note: Quantify in units and ask how long; a non-judgemental tone gets an honest answer.

exchanges.ask: How long have you been drinking like this?
exchanges.reply: About twenty years. It went up after I started driving at night.

exchanges.ask: Have you ever felt you should cut down, or woken up needing a drink?
exchanges.reply: My wife has asked me to cut down many times. In the mornings I sometimes shake until I have a drink.
exchanges.note: CAGE-style questions; morning drinking suggests dependence.

exchanges.ask: When did you last drink?
exchanges.reply: Four days ago, before I came in.

exchanges.ask: Do you smoke, or use any other substances?
exchanges.reply: I smoke ten cigarettes a day. No other drugs.

exchanges.ask: Is there any liver disease, jaundice or cancer in the family?
exchanges.reply: My father had a yellow illness and died, but I don't know the cause.

exchanges.ask: How is this affecting you at home and at work?
exchanges.reply: I can't drive now. My wife is worried about money.

differentials.supporting: Twenty years of heavy drinking, ascites, oedema, jaundice, gynaecomastia and day-night reversal.
differentials.against: Other causes can coexist, and alcohol hepatitis could sit on top of cirrhosis.

differentials.diagnosis: Chronic viral hepatitis (B or C) with cirrhosis
differentials.supporting: A family history of a 'yellow illness' and no vaccination; viral and alcohol injury often coexist.
differentials.against: No transfusion, tattoos or injections reported.
Heavy alcohol intake explains the picture better.

differentials.supporting: Weight loss, decompensation over a few months and appetite loss.
differentials.against: Needs imaging; it complicates cirrhosis rather than replacing it.
Jaundice, ascites and stigmata of chronic liver disease point to the liver.

initialManagement: Assess airway, breathing and circulation, check glucose and look for bleeding or sepsis.
Do a diagnostic ascitic tap and send liver tests, clotting, FBC, U&E and cultures.
Start thiamine and monitor for alcohol withdrawal.
Review for hepatic encephalopathy and treat any trigger.

items: Resuscitate and treat any bleeding or infection; give antibiotics for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
Thiamine, and a withdrawal scale such as CIWA with benzodiazepines if needed.
Sodium restriction and spironolactone with a loop diuretic; therapeutic paracentesis with albumin for tense ascites.
Endoscopic screening for varices and non-selective beta-blocker or band ligation.
Treat the cause: complete alcohol abstinence and support.
Ultrasound surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma about every six months.
Vaccination against hepatitis A and B, and nutritional support.
Alcohol cessation programme and family involvement; consider referral for liver transplantation.

keyPoints: Ascites, jaundice and encephalopathy mark decompensation.
Take a quantified, non-judgemental alcohol history.
Always ask about bleeding, confusion and last drink.
osceTips: Open with the patient's own words and clarify each symptom.
Ask the negatives that change management: haematemesis, melaena, fever, confusion.
Summarise at the end and offer a clear differential.

items: Introduces self, confirms identity and obtains consent
Asks the patient to describe the problem in their own words
Characterises the abdominal swelling and leg swelling
Asks about jaundice, dark urine, itching and stool colour
Asks about haematemesis, melaena and confusion
Takes a quantified alcohol history, including the last drink
Asks about transfusions, tattoos, injections and family history
Asks about the effect on home and work
Summarises the history and offers a differential

questions.q: What features suggest this patient is decompensated?
questions.a: Ascites, jaundice and encephalopathy, and a history of variceal bleeding if present.

questions.q: How would you quantify alcohol intake?
questions.a: Ask the drink, the volume and how often, convert to units, and ask how long and when the last drink was.
Chronic alcohol use depletes thiamine, and treating it early prevents Wernicke's encephalopathy.
